issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-related trigger content is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. Ambulances is coherent for medical trauma, but military topics suggests a very different trauma context and is therefore clinically implausible here.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: Revenge/get-even rumination implies an identifiable perpetrator or assailant. That does not fit a child's life-threatening illness trauma, which is not typically organized around interpersonal assault. This creates a cross-node/content mismatch with the trauma type.

issues.item: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/childbirth/babies is not a clearly coherent trigger for trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness unless the illness was specifically neonatal/perinatal, which is not indicated. In this profile it sits awkwardly alongside the more plausible medical trigger of ambulances.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Physical self-harm used to stop thinking about the event is possible in PTSD, but here it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile: the only triggers are situational reminders, with no corroborating threat, appraisal, or memory items suggesting the kind of overwhelming internal distress usually linked to this strategy. Given the formulation, maladaptive strategies should connect plausibly back to the listed triggers; this item is poorly matched.

issues.item: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: The revenge/assailant rumination item is clinically incoherent with the trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, which does not involve an identifiable assailant in the usual sense. This item also fails to link plausibly with the selected trigger profile (ambulances, medical procedures, sleeping alone) and does not fit the formulation, where the active pattern is a reciprocal Triggers ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop centered on trigger-driven coping rather than interpersonal retaliation.

issues.explanation: 'Revenge against assailant' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, which typically lacks a personal perpetrator. This item implies an assaultive trauma context that does not fit the validated trauma type.

issues.explanation: 'I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay' is a weaker fit than reassurance focused on the child's health/safety. In the context of trauma centered on a child's illness, this wording shifts the threat target to the self without support from any threat, memory, or appraisal items.

vignette:
Rajan is a 50-year-old South Asian American animator, married for twenty-three years, who was referred for psychological assessment following a prolonged period of distress that he traces back to a single, devastating stretch of time roughly two years ago, when his youngest son was admitted to the intensive care unit with a diagnosis of acute bacterial meningitis. The boy was seven years old. For eleven days, Rajan slept in a reclining chair beside the hospital bed, watching nurses adjust IV lines, listening to monitors, breathing in the sharp, antiseptic smell that permeated every corridor. On the fourth night, the attending physician pulled him aside and told him, with careful professional restraint, that the next forty-eight hours would be critical. Rajan stood in the hallway under fluorescent light and understood, for the first time in his life, that his child might die. His son survived, and recovered fully. Rajan has not.

In the months that followed the discharge, Rajan began noticing that certain things undid him in ways he could not explain to his wife or to himself. The smell of antiseptic - encountered when he accompanied his son to a routine pediatric follow-up, or when a colleague at the animation studio mentioned using hand sanitizer - would arrive before he had time to brace, pulling him back to that corridor, that fluorescent light, that carefully restrained voice. Medical appointments of any kind, including his own annual physical, became almost impossible to attend. He sat in waiting rooms certain that the examination itself would confirm something catastrophic, that the ordinary rituals of clinical care were preludes to another crisis. When business travel required him to stay in a hotel room alone, the unfamiliarity of the space - the wrong sounds, the wrong light, the absence of his wife beside him - would stretch into sleeplessness, his mind running over every worst-case scenario he could construct, as though thorough mental preparation might protect him from outcomes he could no longer trust the world to withhold.

It is this last habit that has come to govern much of Rajan's inner life. When a trigger strikes - the smell, a stethoscope, the silence of an unfamiliar room - he finds himself almost immediately rehearsing catastrophe: his son relapsing, a new diagnosis, something missed. He had come to believe, with a logic that felt entirely reasonable to him, that if he thought through the worst in sufficient detail, he would not be ambushed by it again. The rehearsal felt like vigilance, like responsible fatherhood. But the rehearsal itself, playing out in vivid, granular detail, kept the sense of threat alive and immediate, so that the next time he encountered the hospital smell on a colleague's hands, or found himself alone in a hotel room during a conference, the triggers landed with undiminished force. The loop had tightened over months without his noticing: the triggers feeding the mental rehearsal, the rehearsal ensuring that no trigger ever lost its potency.

Alongside this, Rajan frequently seeks reassurance from his wife, calling her from work to confirm that the children are well, asking her repeatedly whether she thinks his own health is stable. She answers patiently, though the calls have increased in frequency, and she has begun gently suggesting that he speak to someone. At the studio, his concentration has suffered. He works alone for long stretches, animating sequences that require sustained imaginative focus, and colleagues have noticed that he is slower to deliver, quicker to apologise, and rarely stays for the informal conversations that once anchored his working day. There is also, present but not central to the picture, a strand of bitter anger he has not spoken about to anyone: a recurring, almost obsessive preoccupation with the hospital administrator who he felt dismissed his questions during those eleven days, a rumination about accountability, about what it would mean to make that indifference felt.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a panic response during his own medical examination last month - a routine blood draw that he could not complete. He left the clinic without explanation, sat in his car for forty minutes, and drove home. He is most afraid, he said at intake, that he will never stop waiting for something terrible to happen. What he hopes for, more quietly, is to sleep beside his wife without checking, in the dark, whether his son is still breathing.
